title: Paralytic Ileus
subject: Surgery
summary: Paralytic ileus is a functional bowel obstruction caused by loss of intestinal motility. It is common after abdominal surgery and in low‑resource settings where infections, electrolyte disturbances, and herbal toxins are frequent.

sections.p: A reversible cessation of peristalsis without a mechanical blockage. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by plain abdominal radiograph showing uniformly dilated loops of bowel with air‑fluid levels and absent transition point.
b: Absence of a palpable mass or hernia
No evidence of obstruction on contrast study if performed

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical and radiologic criteria:
b: Mild: mild distension, tolerates oral fluids, no systemic signs
Moderate: marked distension, vomiting, mild tachycardia, leukocytosis
Severe: hemodynamic instability, peritonitis, metabolic acidosis, or failure to improve after 48 h

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals the most common precipitants are:
b: Post‑operative handling of the bowel (especially after laparotomy)
Severe electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia)
Intra‑abdominal infection (peritonitis, intra‑abdominal abscess, TB peritonitis)
Systemic infection/sepsis (malaria, HIV‑related opportunistic infection)
Drugs: opioids, anticholinergics, quinine, traditional herbal preparations

sections.p: Patients lie supine with a distended, tympanic abdomen. Early ileus may have hyperactive, high‑pitched bowel sounds; later the sounds become absent.
b: Nausea and bilious vomiting
Abdominal pain that is diffuse, not localized
Absence of flatus or stool passage
Visible peristaltic waves may be absent

t.b: Does the patient have a mechanical obstruction? → Uniformly dilated loops without a transition point support paralytic ileus.
Are electrolyte derangements contributing? → Low K+ or Mg2+ explains motility loss; replace accordingly.
Is there infection or inflammation? → Leukocytosis or left shift suggests intra‑abdominal sepsis needing antibiotics.
Can we exclude a mass or fluid collection? → Dilated, static loops with absent peristalsis favour ileus.

sections.p: Failure to resolve may progress to bowel ischemia, perforation, or sepsis.
b: Persistent abdominal pain with guarding or rebound → possible perforation
Increasing lactate or metabolic acidosis → ischemia
Uncontrolled sepsis (fever > 38.5 °C, HR > 120, hypotension)
Signs of abdominal compartment syndrome (tight abdomen, oliguria, rising ventilatory pressures)

sections.p: Treat the precipitating factor, then support gut motility and prevent complications.
b: Correct electrolytes: give IV potassium chloride to keep K+ ≥ 4.0 mmol/L; replace magnesium if < 0.7 mmol/L.
Stop offending drugs: discontinue opioids, anticholinergics, quinine, and herbal extracts.
Nasogastric decompression if vomiting or marked distension.
Early ambulation and gentle bedside mobilization to stimulate peristalsis.
IV fluids: isotonic crystalloids to maintain euvolemia; avoid fluid overload in patients with cardiac disease.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole).
Consider pro‑kinetic agents (e.g., metoclopramide) only when no contraindication; avoid in patients with seizure risk.

sections.p: Monitor bowel sounds, abdominal girth, and fluid balance every 4 h. Remove NG tube once bowel sounds return and patient tolerates oral intake.
b: Educate patients on early mobilization after surgery.
Avoid routine postoperative opioid use; use multimodal analgesia.
Check electrolytes daily in the first 48 h post‑op.
Screen for TB or HIV in patients with chronic peritonitis.

sections.p: Conditions that also cause abdominal distension and absent bowel sounds.
b: Mechanical small‑bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia, tumour)
Large‑bowel obstruction (colonic cancer, volvulus)
Perforated viscus with peritonitis (pain is more localized, guarding present)
Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion, lactate rise)

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite serious disease.
b: Normal abdominal X‑ray early in ileus – repeat after 12 h if clinical picture worsens.
Leukocytosis may be absent in immunocompromised (HIV) patients; rely on clinical signs.
Electrolyte levels can be falsely normal if drawn after aggressive IV replacement; repeat if suspicion remains.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening abdominal pain with guarding or rigidity
New onset fever > 38.5 °C with rising lactate

faq.q: Why does paralytic ileus cause absent bowel sounds?
faq.a: Loss of coordinated smooth‑muscle contractions stops peristalsis, so no audible activity.

faq.q: Can oral fluids be given early?
faq.a: Only after bowel sounds return and the patient tolerates small sips without vomiting.

faq.q: Is surgery ever needed for paralytic ileus?
faq.a: Only if a mechanical obstruction is discovered or if perforation/ischemia develops.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order for a postoperative patient with a distended abdomen and no bowel sounds? — Plain abdominal X‑ray to differentiate paralytic ileus from mechanical obstruction.
A patient on high‑dose morphine develops ileus. How do you modify his analgesia and why? — Switch to non‑opioid analgesics and regional techniques; opioids depress gut motility.

How do you distinguish paralytic ileus from a small‑bowel obstruction on clinical exam? — Ileus shows diffuse pain, absent bowel sounds, and uniform loop dilation; obstruction often has localized pain, high‑pitched hyperactive sounds early, and a transition point on imaging.
Which electrolyte abnormality most commonly precipitates ileus and how do you correct it? — Hypokalemia; replace potassium intravenously to keep serum ≥ 4.0 mmol/L.
A patient with HIV presents with abdominal distension and ileus‑like picture. What additional cause should you consider? — Tuberculous peritonitis; obtain acid‑fast stain or PCR if possible.
When is nasogastric decompression indicated in ileus and what are its risks? — Indicated for persistent vomiting or marked distension; risks include nasal trauma and aspiration if tube is misplaced.
What red‑flag sign would prompt immediate surgical review in a patient with presumed ileus? — Development of peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound) suggesting perforation or ischemia.
Why are pro‑kinetic drugs used cautiously in ileus? — They may lower seizure threshold or cause extrapyramidal side effects; avoid in patients with CNS disease.
